findings.source_passage: Through its inexpressible, strange eyes, methought I peeped to secrets which took hold of God. As Abraham before the angels, I bowed myself; the white thing was so white, its wings so wide, and in those for ever exiled waters, I had lost the miserable warping memories of traditions and of towns.
findings.source_locator: albatross footnote, after 'cries, as some king's ghost in supernatural distress'
findings.why_it_matters: The draft preserves 'peeped to secrets which took hold of God' and 'As Abraham before the angels, I bowed myself' but omits the pivotal closing phrase 'the white thing was so white, its wings so wide, and in those for ever exiled waters, I had lost the miserable warping memories of traditions and of towns.' This is one of the most poetically distinctive and critically cited sentences in the entire chapter, capturing the erasure of civilization in the presence of the sublime; its loss is a major voice and interpretive failure.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore verbatim: 'the white thing was so white, its wings so wide, and in those for ever exiled waters, I had lost the miserable warping memories of traditions and of towns.' This sentence must appear in full.

findings.source_passage: whiteness is not so much a colour as the visible absence of colour; and at the same time the concrete of all colours; is it for these reasons that there is such a dumb blankness, full of meaning, in a wide landscape of snows—a colourless, all-colour of atheism from which we shrink?
findings.source_locator: penultimate paragraph, 'Is it that by its indefiniteness…'
findings.why_it_matters: The draft retains this passage almost verbatim, which is good, but the preceding clause about 'the heartless voids and immensities of the universe, and thus stabs us from behind with the thought of annihilation' is compressed to 'stabbing us with annihilation at the sight of the milky way,' losing the critically important phrase 'stabs us from behind'—a signature rhetorical construction that conveys ambush and the unconscious, which the critical tradition specifically examines.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'stabs us from behind with the thought of annihilation' verbatim; the preposition and bodily metaphor are load-bearing.

findings.source_passage: Not Coleridge first threw that spell; but God's great, unflattering laureate, Nature.
findings.why_it_matters: The draft runs 'Not Coleridge first threw that spell; but God's great, unflattering laureate, Nature' as a sentence fragment grafted awkwardly after a colon following 'lurks the spell;'—destroying its rhetorical independence and punch. The source deploys this as a standalone, epigrammatic sentence that redirects literary authority from Coleridge to Nature; the draft's syntactic fusion flattens it into a subordinate clause.
findings.suggested_fix: Make 'Not Coleridge first threw that spell; but God's great, unflattering laureate, Nature.' a fully independent sentence as in the source.

findings.source_passage: giving the white man ideal mastership over every dusky tribe
findings.why_it_matters: The draft retains this phrase but strips it from its full rhetorical position within the immense accumulative 'though…though…though' syntactic structure. The entire single-sentence catalogue is one of the most discussed formal achievements of the chapter—the draft compresses the catalogue into a list, destroying its anaphoric architecture and the slow build that makes the ultimate reversal ('yet…strikes more of panic') devastating.
findings.suggested_fix: Even at compression, preserve the anaphoric 'though…though' sentence structure for at least four or five entries so the rhetorical pivot ('yet for all these accumulated associations') lands properly.

findings.source_passage: No: but here thou beholdest even in a dumb brute, the instinct of the knowledge of the demonism in the world.
findings.source_locator: colt passage, after Vermont colt paragraph
findings.why_it_matters: The draft renders this as 'Here behold, even in a brute, the instinct of the demonism in the world,' dropping 'the knowledge of'—a critical three words that distinguish mere instinct from a deeper epistemological claim about innate knowledge of evil. The phrase 'instinct of the knowledge of the demonism' is philosophically precise and interpretively weighty; its compression changes the meaning.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'the instinct of the knowledge of the demonism in the world' verbatim.

findings.source_passage: Why to the man of untutored ideality, who happens to be but loosely acquainted with the peculiar character of the day, does the bare mention of Whitsuntide marshal in the fancy such long, dreary, speechless processions of slow-pacing pilgrims, down-cast and hooded with new-fallen snow?
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'Why to the man of untutored ideality'
findings.why_it_matters: The entire 'Whitsuntide / White Friar / White Nun / White Tower / White Mountains / White Sea / Yellow Sea / tall pale man of the Hartz' sequence is a sustained voice-establishing rhetorical interrogation that exemplifies Ishmael's digressive, associative consciousness at its most distinctive. The draft collapses it to a single summary sentence ('Name alone can summon a spectralness: the White Tower; the White Mountains; the White Sea…'). The loss of Whitsuntide, White Friar, and the Yellow Sea contrast ('lulls us with mortal thoughts of long lacquered mild afternoons') is particularly severe.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore at minimum the Whitsuntide question and the Yellow Sea contrast ('while that of the Yellow Sea lulls us with mortal thoughts of long lacquered mild afternoons'), which are the most rhetorically distinctive entries in the sequence.

findings.source_passage: all deified Nature absolutely paints like the harlot, whose allurements cover nothing but the charnel-house within
findings.why_it_matters: The draft retains this phrase but the full surrounding argument—'every stately or lovely emblazoning—the sweet tinges of sunset skies and woods; yea, and the gilded velvets of butterflies, and the butterfly cheeks of young girls; all these are but subtile deceits'—is compressed to 'sunset tinges, butterfly cheeks.' The loss of 'the gilded velvets of butterflies' and the full appositive structure weakens the harlot simile's preparatory build.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'the sweet tinges of sunset skies and woods; yea, and the gilded velvets of butterflies, and the butterfly cheeks of young girls' before the harlot sentence.

summary: The draft contains three high-severity failures—the erasure of the climactic albatross sentence ('the white thing was so white, its wings so wide…warping memories of traditions and of towns'), the syntactic crippling of 'Not Coleridge first threw that spell,' and the blunting of 'stabs us from behind'—plus four medium failures including the near-total collapse of the Whitsuntide/White Sea rhetorical interrogation sequence, making regeneration mandatory.
